resolved_by: Supreme Court, United States v. Taylor, 596 U.S. 845 (2022), which affirmed the Fourth Circuit's Taylor decision and held that attempted Hobbs Act robbery is not a crime of violence under § 924(c) because an attempt must itself involve actual, attempted, or threatened force.
issue: Is an attempt to commit an offense that can be completed by threatened force automatically a crime of violence under 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), or must the attempt itself involve the attempted use of physical force?

sides.position: Any attempt to commit a crime of violence is invariably a crime of violence, because § 924(c) reaches attempted use of force.
cases: United States v. Walker, 990 F.3d 316 (3d Cir. 2021)
United States v. Smith, 957 F.3d 590 (5th Cir. 2020)
United States v. Ingram, 947 F.3d 1021 (7th Cir. 2020)
United States v. Dominguez, 954 F.3d 1251 (9th Cir. 2020)
United States v. St. Hubert, 909 F.3d 335 (11th Cir. 2018)

sides.position: An attempt is a crime of violence only if the attempt itself involves actual, attempted, or threatened force; an attempt to threaten force is not an attempt to use force.
cases: United States v. Taylor, 979 F.3d 203 (4th Cir. 2020), aff'd, 596 U.S. 845 (2022)
United States v. Nixon, No. 21-4334 (4th Cir. 2024)

this_court: This court follows the Supreme Court's Taylor rule that an attempt must itself involve actual, attempted, or threatened force; the split is described as historical and resolved.
quote: Our decision in Taylor created a split with our sister circuits, and the Supreme Court promptly took up the case.
cite: United States v. Eric Nixon, No. 21-4334 (4th Cir. 2024)
